antipatterns: app/Console/Commands/CountInactiveUsers.php:24 – prints a bare number. It gets appended to a shared log with no label or timestamp, so the log line '2' says nothing about what was counted, which works against the 'shows up in our logs' goal
tests/Feature/CountInactiveUsersTest.php:48-54 – the schedule test asserts only the cron expression. It never checks that output is sent to a log file, and that is the stated purpose of the schedule
tests/Feature/CountInactiveUsersTest.php:14,24,30 – uses assertExitCode(0)/assertExitCode(1) where assertSuccessful()/assertFailed() would be more expressive
tests/Feature/CountInactiveUsersTest.php:6-25 – time is only frozen in the boundary test. The other tests depend on 1-day margins, so they are safe, but this is inconsistent
tests/Feature/CountInactiveUsersTest.php:50 – the closure parameter has no type
tests/Feature/CountInactiveUsersTest.php:46 – the dataset has no labels, so failing cases are harder to read
strengths: Uses a modern #[Scope] attribute scope with a correctly grouped whereNull/orWhere closure, so the OR does not leak into other conditions
Uses the #[Signature]/#[Description] command attributes (verified present in the installed framework)
Validates --days with FILTER_VALIDATE_INT. Probe: '' and 'abc' are rejected; '0' is accepted and counts everyone not logged in at this exact moment, which is a defensible reading
Uses the Schedule facade in routes/console.php with dailyAt('06:00') and appendOutputTo, which is proportionate for a single server
Tests the strict-boundary case (exactly 90 days counts as active)

antipatterns: database/migrations/2026_11_07_190122_add_last_login_at_to_users_table.php:12 – ->after() only works on MySQL. It is harmless elsewhere but adds ceremony
app/Console/Commands/CountInactiveUsers.php:19 – uses $this->error rather than $this->components->error (minor styling inconsistency with modern commands)
app/Console/Commands/CountInactiveUsers.php:18 – rejects --days=0. This is a defensible choice but stricter than the spec requires
strengths: Prints a labelled line ('Users inactive for 90 days: N'), so entries in the appended log file are self-describing
The schedule test asserts both the cron expression and the log destination (storage_path('logs/inactive-users.log'))
beforeEach freezeTime makes every date-based test deterministic
Covers default, --days, never-logged-in, exact boundary, the empty table, and a labelled invalid-input dataset (zero/negative/text/decimal) using assertSuccessful/assertFailed
Uses the same clean #[Scope] attribute scope with a grouped OR closure, plus the #[Signature]/#[Description] attributes and the datetime cast
Probes: whitespace-padded ' 7 ' is accepted, a huge --days value works, and 0 is rejected with exit 1 and a clear message

v.rationale: I reviewed impl-2 first, then impl-1. The two are almost identical: both add the column, the same #[Scope] attribute scope with a grouped OR, the same attribute-based command, and the same schedule entry (dailyAt('06:00') with appendOutputTo). Both full suites pass (impl-2 12/12, impl-1 11/11). My throwaway probes ('0', a huge value, whitespace, the empty string, text, decimals) found no real bugs in either; I deleted the probe files afterwards. The ranking comes down to how well each meets the task's purpose, getting the number into the logs, and how thorough the tests are. impl-2 prints a labelled, self-describing line, while impl-1 appends a bare integer to the log file. impl-2's schedule test checks the output destination, not just the cron expression. impl-2 also freezes time for every test, uses expressive assertSuccessful/assertFailed, and labels its invalid-input dataset. impl-1 accepts --days=0 where impl-2 rejects it; both readings are defensible, so this did not affect the ranking.
